paragraphs.text: Ants have been living in large, highly organized, cooperative societies – practicing activities from strategic army warfare to agriculture and livestock herding - for at least fifty million years. Their colonies are single entities in which individual members function as cells, with specific groups performing separate duties like specialized organs. One particularly striking example of this behavior is provided by the weaver ant species, which acquired its name because it makes soccer-ball-sized nests among tree branches by sewing leaves together.

The beginning of a weaver ant nest-construction project is remarkable. A single worker stands on a leaf and reaches to grasp the edge of another leaf nearby. If the gap is too great, a second worker climbs over the first, and the bottom ant grasps the newcomer by its wire-thin waist and holds it out closer to the goal. Still not enough? A third ant climbs over the first two and is lifted out even farther. Ant by ant, a living chain grows into thin air like the arm of a construction crane. Once the distant leaf is grabbed, the entire group pulls together, often with nest mates that have formed parallel chains and reinforcing cross-links, to draw the leaves' edges together. Workers begin to position themselves along the join between the leaves, legs holding on to one edge, jaws gripping the other. Then, as evening comes on and the humidity rises, more workers arrive from nearby nests carrying larvae that are about to enter the pupal stage and become adults. Rather than spinning a cocoon, as do other ant species' larvae, these give their silk to the colony. Standing over the places where the leaves are touching, an adult uses its antennae to tap the head of the larva it is holding, telling it to produce silk from its salivary glands. This silk acts like a thread with which the ants literally sew the leaves together, thus producing a nest.

Each weaver ant colony inhabits from half a dozen up to a hundred of these extraordinary creations at any given time, forming a sort of city of boroughs and suburbs connected by busy pathways. This whole area is maintained by an ordered group of workers, which spread from treetops to the forest floor, staying in harmony through constant communication. They touch each other, laying down scents with different glands to pass different messages, and also release chemicals into the air to broadcast warnings quickly and widely.

In a completed nest, a queen, many times the size of typical workers, lays thousands of eggs. When the larvae hatch from the eggs, some of the workers feed and clean them and transport a portion of them to nurseries. Every so often a large batch of reproductive females and males is produced. They grow wings and fly off to mate, and a fertilized female may start a fresh colony. The rest of the time, the queen's offspring all become nonbreeding females. Some of these are workers, while others are soldiers who patrol their colony's territory and fight with any invader, no matter how big, no matter how dangerous, in service to the queen and the survival of the colony as a whole.

As predators, weaver ants hunt practically every kind of insect big enough for a meal – and so effectively that the ants' territories, sometimes covering as many as seventeen trees, become patches where many tiny creatures may no longer exist at all. Chinese farmers noticed this 1,700 years ago and placed nests in orchards to safeguard fruit, making weaver ants the oldest known form of 'biocontrol' – fighting pests with animals rather than chemicals. Lately, ecologists have been promoting them in Africa as a safe, effective, and inexpensive alternative to pesticide sprays. The poorest farmer can connect strings from a weaver ant nest to fruit trees and large numbers of female ants will tirelessly eliminate fruit flies, caterpillars and other potential pests for free.

Another extraordinary aspect of weaver ant behavior is the way that groups of them look after a type of sucking bug that feeds on plant juices. The ants physically carry these insects to rich food sources, guard them vigilantly from enemies, and subsequently gather the droplets of sugar-rich syrup, known as honeydew, which the bugs produce. Like every prize, it is then carried off to be shared with nest mates.

Weaver ants weigh so little, they're hardly even affected by gravity. In fact they often don't know which way is down. But if an ant wants to go from one tree to the next, there's a huge gap relative to its size. It might have to travel all the way to the ground, back up again, and then out on another branch. Normally incapable of flight, what they often do is to group together and cross directly to the other side by holding on to each other to form a long chain – truly a remarkable species.
